clue.text: Modest artist right to get replaced by gallery essentially

indicators.note: one thing being replaced by another means a letter is swapped out for a different one

parts.note: L. S. Lowry, the English painter of northern industrial scenes
R is the standard abbreviation for right; this is the letter that goes

indicators.note: the essence of something is its core, so only the central letter of the word is kept

parts.note: the fourth of seven letters, the very centre of the word

explanation.surface: A self-effacing painter has his work moved out of the main room of a gallery.
explanation.walkthrough: Take LOWRY and swap its R for L to get LOWLY. Lowry, famous for matchstick figures, is a favourite crossword artist.
explanation.definitionFit: Lowly and modest are synonyms describing humble rank or a lack of pretension.

clue.text: Place with tiny population?

parts.note: surface reading: a hamlet or village where very few people live
setter's reading: a place whose inhabitants are themselves tiny, as in Swift's Gulliver's Travels

explanation.walkthrough: A tiny population normally means few people; here it means people who are tiny, the six-inch islanders Gulliver meets.
explanation.definitionFit: Swift's fictional island is inhabited entirely by miniature people, so its whole population is literally small in stature.

clue.text: Revelry witnessed going north on voyage

indicators.note: in a down clue, one piece sitting on another means it is placed above it
in a down clue, travelling north means reading upwards, so the letters run the other way

parts.note: to witness something is to see it; past tense
a sail is a trip by boat

explanation.surface: Merrymaking was seen heading north on a sea voyage.
explanation.walkthrough: In a down clue, going north turns a word upside down, and 'on' puts the first piece above the second.
explanation.definitionFit: Wassail is old-fashioned festive drinking and carousing, especially at Christmas, so it is a form of revelry.

clue.text: State formerly guy's viola playing aggravated at first

indicators.note: playing suggests letters in motion, performing in a new arrangement

parts.note: the possessive taken as plain letters
taken as written

indicators.note: at first points to the opening letter of the word just before it

parts.note: the opening letter

explanation.surface: A man's viola playing used to be irritating at the start.
explanation.walkthrough: 'State formerly' sits at the front, disguised as the start of a sentence; the apostrophe in guy’s is ignored.
explanation.definitionFit: The Balkan federation broke up in the 1990s, so it is a nation that no longer exists.

clue.text: One reading lines describing saint, composer of hymns

indicators.note: to describe a shape is to draw round it, so one thing is drawn around another

parts.note: a palm reader studies the lines on a hand
S is the abbreviation for saint

explanation.surface: A churchgoer reads lines about a saint who wrote hymns.
explanation.walkthrough: 'One reading lines' suggests an actor or lector, but here the lines are on a palm.
explanation.definitionFit: A psalmist writes psalms, the sacred songs of the Bible, which are hymns in the broad sense.

clue.text: Will novelist this writer's left barely suppress conceit?

indicators.note: something bare is stripped of its covering, so the word loses its outside letters

parts.note: Will Self is an English novelist
the setter speaking of himself: I am, shortened to I'M
port is the nautical word for the left side of a ship
to cancel is to suppress or call off

explanation.surface: Will a novelist like me be able to hold back his own vanity?
explanation.walkthrough: 'Will' looks like a verb opening a question but is the novelist's first name. CANCEL without its outer letters leaves ANCE.
explanation.definitionFit: Conceit means an inflated opinion of oneself, which is exactly what an exaggerated sense of one's own importance is.

clue.text: Crowd losing belief finally in rugby player

indicators.note: to lose something is to be without it, so a letter is dropped

parts.note: a flock is a crowd, of sheep or of churchgoers

indicators.note: finally points to the closing letter of the word before it

parts.note: the final letter, which is removed

explanation.surface: Spectators lose faith in a rugby player at the end of a match.
explanation.walkthrough: FLOCK without its F leaves the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: In rugby union the two locks are second-row forwards in the scrum, so a lock is a player position.

clue.text: Fire unspecified number, about to rise, breaking word

indicators.note: breaking into something means getting inside it

parts.note: word in the sense of news or information
n is the algebraic symbol for an indefinite number

indicators.note: in a down clue, rising means reading from bottom to top

parts.note: re means about or concerning

explanation.surface: Sack an unknown number of staff, about to rise up and break their word.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Fire' reads as dismissing people but is the definition; 'word' means news, as in 'send word'.
explanation.definitionFit: An inferno is a large, raging blaze, so it is a synonym for a fire of great intensity.

clue.text: Brief letter secretary encloses

indicators.note: a phrase that encloses something holds it inside, spanning the words

parts.note: the run of letters straddling the two words

explanation.surface: A short note that a secretary puts in an envelope.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface wants a brief letter and secretary as abbreviations; instead the answer sits across the join of the two words.
explanation.definitionFit: Terse and brief are synonyms for speech or writing using few words, often abruptly.

clue.text: Reactionary person performing lament Ann heard

indicators.note: performing means acting out, so the letters put on a show in a fresh order

parts.note: taken as written
taken as written
taken as written

explanation.surface: Someone singing a lament was heard by Ann.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Heard' looks like a sound-alike signal, but it is simply part of the letters to be rearranged.
explanation.definitionFit: Neanderthal is used figuratively for someone with primitive, backward-looking views, so a hidebound reactionary fits.

clue.text: Way to keep dip in dish

indicators.note: to keep something is to hold it inside

parts.note: a lane is a way or narrow road
a sag is a dip or sinking

explanation.surface: How to stop a dip sinking into a dish.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Dip' suggests a sauce served with food, but here it is a downward sag.
explanation.definitionFit: Lasagne is an Italian baked pasta course, a familiar example of a dish.

clue.text: Back sporting official in charge given extremely unusual match

indicators.note: going back means travelling the other way, so everything reads in reverse

parts.note: short for referee
IC is the standard abbreviation for in charge

indicators.note: the extremes of a word are its two ends, so only its outer letters are kept

parts.note: first and last letters

explanation.surface: Support a referee overseeing a very strange sporting fixture.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Match' sounds like a game, carried by the sporting surface, but it is the thing you strike to make a flame.
explanation.definitionFit: Lucifer is an old name for a friction match, from the early brand of strike-anywhere matches.

clue.text: Not present in capital, Stanley sobs at Neil, regularly upset

indicators.note: upset means overturned, so the string is read backwards

parts.note: capital means excellent, i.e. A1, with the 1 written as the letter I

indicators.note: regularly means at fixed intervals, so every other letter is taken

parts.note: the second, fourth, sixth letters and so on

explanation.surface: Absent from the Falklands capital Stanley, someone weeps at Neil's departure.
explanation.walkthrough: Stanley is the capital of the Falkland Islands, which makes 'capital' look like its label; really capital means first-rate, A1.
explanation.definitionFit: In absentia is Latin for 'in absence', used of something done while the person concerned is not there.

clue.text: Genuine hit for Spandau Ballet

definitions.meaning: second meaning: the British band's 1983 number one single

explanation.walkthrough: Spandau Ballet were a 1980s British New Romantic pop group; their best-known ballad was a chart-topper with this title.
explanation.definitionFit: The adjective means real or authentic, and the band's signature 1983 song carries exactly that one-word title.

clue.text: Furore over Conservative getting vulgar, source of downfall?

indicators.note: in a down clue, one thing over another is placed above it

parts.note: a storm is an uproar or furore
C is the abbreviation for Conservative
loud means garish or vulgar, as of clothes

explanation.surface: An outcry over a Tory's crude remarks could bring about his fall.
explanation.walkthrough: The downfall is rain, not a politician's fall; the question mark flags the pun.
explanation.definitionFit: A storm cloud is what heavy rain pours out of, and a downpour is jokingly called a downfall.

clue.text: Collecting daughter one time leaving laundrette Pole runs in E10

indicators.note: to collect something is to take it in and hold it
colours that run spread out of place, so the letters move around
something leaving goes away, so a letter is removed

parts.note: a single T, the abbreviation for time
taken as written
taken as written
D is the abbreviation for daughter

explanation.surface: A Polish man picks up his daughter after a spell at a laundrette in an east London postcode.
explanation.walkthrough: E10 looks like a London postcode (it is Leyton), but it is the definition. Add D to LAUNDRETTE and POLE, drop one T, and rearrange.
explanation.definitionFit: E10 is the British pump label for standard petrol blended with up to ten per cent ethanol, sold as unleaded.

clue.text: Scraps inequality involving soldiers close to retirement

indicators.note: to involve is to include, so one part is taken inside another

parts.note: odds as in a disparity, the odds being stacked against someone
men in the sense of ordinary soldiers

indicators.note: the close of a word is its end, so only the last letter is used

parts.note: the final letter

explanation.surface: An unfair system for soldiers is scrapped as they approach retirement.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Scraps' reads as a verb about abolishing something, but it is a plural noun for leftovers.
explanation.definitionFit: Oddments are leftover bits and pieces, odds and ends, which are scraps of material or stock.

clue.text: Determine priest lacking English somehow gets wrongly understood

indicators.note: somehow means in some unspecified way, so the letters fall into an unpredictable order
lacking something means being without it, so a letter goes

parts.note: taken as written
taken as written
E is the abbreviation for English; it is the letter removed

explanation.surface: Establishing that a clergyman who doesn't speak English is somehow misunderstood.
explanation.walkthrough: DETERMINE drops one E, then joins PRIEST for the rearrangement.
explanation.definitionFit: To misinterpret something is to take its meaning wrongly, so the past participle means understood incorrectly.

clue.text: Ignoring signs at intervals traveller is repeating

indicators.note: to ignore something is to leave it out

parts.note: an itinerant is someone who travels from place to place

indicators.note: at intervals means spaced out, so every other letter is taken

parts.note: the second and fourth letters, which are removed

explanation.surface: A traveller keeps going round, missing every other road sign.
explanation.walkthrough: Remove IN from ITINERANT. The answer is a rare word, Latin-derived like 'iterate'.
explanation.definitionFit: Iterant means doing something again and again, from the same root as iterate and reiterate.

clue.text: Like certain sandals, see lots about

indicators.note: about can mean all over the place, so the letters are scattered into a new order

parts.note: taken as written
taken as written

explanation.surface: Look at all the sandals of a certain kind lying around.
explanation.walkthrough: 'About' looks like a word for lying around, but it rearranges the two words before it.
explanation.definitionFit: Many sandals leave the front of the foot bare, so they are open at the front without any covering for the digits.

clue.text: Musician appears heartless in dock

indicators.note: without a heart means the central letter is taken out

parts.note: a piper plays the bagpipes

explanation.surface: A cruel musician is put on trial in the dock.
explanation.walkthrough: 'In dock' suggests a courtroom, but the dock is a landing stage.
explanation.definitionFit: A pier is a structure where boats tie up, a jetty or landing stage, which is one sense of dock.

clue.text: Republic's creator, from anecdotal proof around

indicators.note: turned around means facing the opposite way
taking something from a phrase means lifting a run of its letters out

parts.note: the run of letters across the end of one word and the start of the next

explanation.surface: Who founded the republic, judging from hearsay evidence?
explanation.walkthrough: 'Republic' looks like a nation, but it is the title of a book.
explanation.definitionFit: The Greek philosopher wrote the Republic, his dialogue about justice and the ideal state, so he is its author.

clue.text: Sauce of American boy in film franchise

indicators.note: in means placed inside something else

parts.note: the slasher horror film series begun in 1996
A is the abbreviation for American
a lad is a boy

explanation.surface: The cheek of an American kid starring in a movie series.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Sauce' reads as impudence, but it is the definition. Salad cream is a tangy British dressing, like a thin mayonnaise.
explanation.definitionFit: Salad cream is a bottled creamy dressing, which counts as a sauce or condiment.

clue.text: Picked up very French café item?

indicators.note: to pick up a sound is to hear it, so the word is judged by ear

parts.note: the French word for very, said aloud

explanation.surface: Someone collects a very French snack at a café.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Picked up' suggests lifting something off a café counter; it signals listening.
explanation.definitionFit: Waiters carry orders on a flat board with a rim, a standard piece of café equipment.

clue.text: Ever clear he's mistaken one for Rachel Reeves!

definitions.text: Ever clear he's mistaken one for Rachel Reeves!

parts.words: Ever clear he's mistaken one for Rachel Reeves!
parts.note: surface reading: someone always clearly confuses a man with the Chancellor
setter's reading: these twelve letters, jumbled, spell the politician's name exactly

explanation.walkthrough: Rachel Reeves is the UK Chancellor of the Exchequer. The letters of 'Ever clear he's' are those of her name rearranged, so the phrase is one of these word puzzles.
explanation.definitionFit: A word or phrase made by rearranging all the letters of another is the term for this kind of letter play.

clue.text: Almost suffer defeat against cricket side following century

indicators.note: one thing following another comes after it in the line

parts.note: C is the Roman numeral for a hundred
to lose is to be defeated
the on side is the leg side of a cricket field

explanation.surface: A cricket team nearly loses after one batter scores a hundred.
explanation.walkthrough: A century in cricket is a hundred runs, but the letter comes from the Roman numeral. The on side is the half of the field behind a batter's legs.
explanation.definitionFit: Close on is an idiom meaning nearly or approximately, as in close on a thousand people.

clue.text: Detached when sunbathing perhaps after cycling

indicators.note: cycling means going round, so letters at the end come round to the front

parts.note: a sunbather is typically lying out in the open

explanation.surface: Feeling detached while sunbathing after a bike ride.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Cycling' suggests a bike ride; it means moving the last three letters round to the front.
explanation.definitionFit: Outlying places are remote and set apart from the centre, so they are detached from the main settlement.

clue.text: Deer injected with small medicinal amounts

indicators.note: something injected goes inside, so one part is pushed into another

parts.note: does are female deer; plural
S is the abbreviation for small

explanation.surface: Deer being given small injections of medicine.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Deer' is plural here.
explanation.definitionFit: A dose is a measured quantity of a drug taken at one time, so doses are amounts of medicine.
